gâteau.etymology_derivation: Old French gastel, from Frankish *wastil. English 'gateau' narrowed to a rich cake; French kept the everyday word — form travels, meaning drifts.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

tu.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the very word the King James Bible still whispers as thou. Point your lips; the vowel is not English's.

je.etymology_derivation: Latin egō → *eo → je. Spanish yo is the sibling; English 'I' descends from the same pronoun by the Germanic road.

le.etymology_derivation: Latin ille 'that one' → il → le. English 'the' walked the same road — both are worn-down pointers.

la.etymology_derivation: ille's feminine illa → la. Before a vowel it loses its a: l'opinion.

un_peu.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus 'a small amount' gave English 'paucity' and French peu — one root, two registers.

collection.etymology_derivation: Latin collectio. The -ION ending is your passport: thousands of nouns cross unchanged — and every one is feminine.

tradition.etymology_derivation: Latin traditio 'a handing over' — a tradition is what gets handed over.

confirmation.etymology_derivation: The nasal N is thought, not said: confiRmation with the N half-swallowed.

organisation.etymology_derivation: English spells -ization, French -isation — one S, never a Z, in French.

opinion.etymology_derivation: Latin opinio 'what one supposes'. Starts with a vowel, so la loses its a: l'opinion.

réservation.etymology_derivation: English wrote the accent out; French kept the é so you know where the stress lands.

complication.etymology_derivation: Two nasals, one rule: con- and -tion both think their N without saying it.

passion.etymology_derivation: Latin passio 'suffering' — passion is what you suffer for.

invitation.etymology_derivation: in- + vitare; the invitation is the not-refusing.

confirmer.etymology_derivation: confirmation → confirmer. Strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the verb.

organiser.etymology_derivation: organisation → organiser. One S in French, even where English writes Z.

célébrer.etymology_derivation: célébration → célébrer. The trap: not *célébrater — the whole -ation goes before -er arrives.

participer.context_translation: I want to get involved a little.
participer.etymology_derivation: participation → participer. 'To get involved' sounds formal in English but everyday in French — register travels in reverse.

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

inviter.context_translation: Do you want to invite Marie?

réserver.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.

pas.etymology_derivation: negation grew from ne vais pas un pas — 'I don't go a step'. Pas is literally a footstep, the same word as pace.

ne.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn wore down to ne. The verb sits in a ne...pas sandwich; spoken French often drops the first slice.

être.etymology_derivation: Latin esse 'to be' → essere → être. English kept the root in essence and quintessential — the being-ness inside the word.

cest.english_meaning: it is; this is; that is
cest.etymology_derivation: ce ('that') + est — the elision French performs constantly: a vowel before a vowel loses its tail.

suis.etymology_derivation: je suis is literally 'I follow' — Latin sequor, the root of sequence and sequel. Being is following, historically.

est.shift_rule: Latin est — the same word as English is
est.etymology_derivation: Latin est and English is are the same Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti — the oldest cognate verb pair on either trail.

es.etymology_derivation: Latin es — the very form English's KJV 'thou art' preserves; tu es and thou art are one word.

très.etymology_derivation: Latin trāns 'across' — très means 'beyond, across the line'. English kept the same root in transmit and transatlantic.

université.etymology_derivation: -ity → -ité, and every -ité is feminine. The accent on the é marks the final syllable English swallows.

possibilité.etymology_derivation: Latin possibilitas. The -ty words all convert: ability, activity, university…

différence.etymology_derivation: Latin differentia. The -ance/-ence endings convert whole and are always feminine.

importance.etymology_derivation: in- + portare 'to carry in' — what gets carried in matters.

liberté.etymology_derivation: liberté/liberty — the Norman doublet in -ité form: same Latin liber, two carriers.

est_ce_que.context_phrase: Est-ce que tu veux le gâteau ?
est_ce_que.etymology_derivation: Literally 'is it that you want…' — a question scaffolded out of a statement, no word order changed.

où.etymology_derivation: Latin ubi 'where' — the root English borrowed wholesale in 'ubiquitous' (present everywhere).

pourquoi.etymology_derivation: pour + quoi = 'for what' — English's 'wherefore' (for-what) built the same way: wherefore art thou.

docteur.etymology_derivation: Latin doctor 'teacher'. -or/-er nouns convert to -eur and are usually masculine.

directeur.etymology_derivation: Latin directus 'straight-lined' — the one who keeps things straight.

honneur.etymology_derivation: honour/honneur — a Norman doublet hiding in the -eur family.

couleur.etymology_derivation: Latin color → couleur — feminine, the famous exception the -eur squad warns you about.

cœur.etymology_derivation: Latin cor/cordis — English kept the root in core, courage ('heart'), accord.

bonheur.etymology_derivation: bon 'good' + heur 'fortune' (Latin augurium 'omen' — English 'augury'). Happiness is luck, well met.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

bonjour.etymology_derivation: bon 'good' + jour 'day' (Latin diurnum) — English's 'good day' is the same thought, German's Guten Tag too.

merci.etymology_derivation: Latin mercēs 'wages, reward' — thank-you and mercy are the same coin: what you owe.

oui.etymology_derivation: worn down from Vulgar Latin hoc illud 'yes indeed!' — a yes so emphatic it wore itself into one syllable.

sil_vous_plait.etymology_derivation: 'if it pleases you' — politeness as a small conditional; compare 'if you please', which English still owns.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

jai.etymology_derivation: je + ai with the vowel sacrificed — elision again, the apostrophe marks the cut.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

homme.etymology_derivation: Latin homō 'man' — the root of human, homicide, humus (of the earth). The H is written and never said.

maison.etymology_derivation: Latin mansiō 'a staying' → maison and mansion: the house you stay in, and the big one.

pain.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis 'bread' — a pantry is literally the bread-room. The N is thought, not said: the nasal vowel is the lesson.

eau.shift_rule: Latin aqua, all three vowels are ghosts of a
eau.etymology_derivation: Latin aqua → ea → eau: one syllable wearing two vowels and a consonant as historical scar tissue. Feminine: l'eau.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.

grand.etymology_derivation: English 'grand' came straight from French; the feminine adds a silent -e, which wakes the silent d into sound: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ → grande /ɡʁɑ̃d/.

petit.etymology_derivation: English 'petite' is the French feminine form, borrowed whole — the masculine is petit.

vert.etymology_derivation: Latin viridis → verdant, verdure — the green English kept in poetry.

blanc.etymology_derivation: Germanic blank 'shining white' → French blanc, English blank and blanket (the white cloth).

bleu.shift_rule: Frankish blao — one Germanic word, two languages
bleu.etymology_derivation: Frankish *blao gave English blue and French bleu — a Germanic word inside Romance, no shift needed.

rouge.etymology_derivation: Latin rubeus 'red' — the same stone English calls ruby. Rouge crossed into English as the makeup word.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

je_vais.etymology_derivation: vais is aller's only irregular card in je; with an infinitive after it, it makes the future.

on.context_translation: Shall we go to the café?
on.etymology_derivation: on is worn-down homme — 'the man says' became 'one says' became spoken French's everyday 'we'. The nasal vowel is the fossil.

à.etymology_derivation: Latin ad 'to' — English kept it in adhere, advance, admire. With le it fuses: à + le = au.

de.etymology_derivation: Latin dē 'down from' — of and from in one small word.

chez.etymology_derivation: Latin casa 'hut, house' — the same house English visits in casino (literally 'little house'). No English twin: an honest loss.

avec.etymology_derivation: ab hoc 'by this' wore into avec. No English twin — but 'with' itself once meant 'against', so prepositions travel too.

père.etymology_derivation: Latin pater — the root of paternal, patriarch. English kept the root, French kept the word.

frère.etymology_derivation: Latin frāter — fraternal, friar (the brother of the church).

sœur.etymology_derivation: Latin soror — English kept the Latin sisterhood in sorority.

famille.etymology_derivation: Latin familia was the whole household — servants included. The famulus 'servant' is inside.

deux.etymology_derivation: Latin duo — English duo, deuce (the two-card).

trois.etymology_derivation: Latin trēs and English three share the Proto-Indo-European *treyes — the oldest cognate pair on the trail.

quatre.etymology_derivation: Latin quattuor — quartet, quarter. And quatre-vingts is four twenties: the count of 'four score'.

cinq.etymology_derivation: Latin quinque — quintet, quintessence (the fifth element).

sept.etymology_derivation: Latin septem — September was month seven of the old calendar before January butted in.

huit.shift_rule: Latin octō, o breathed into hu-
huit.etymology_derivation: Latin octō — octopus, October. French breathed an h in front: huit.

neuf.etymology_derivation: Latin novem 'nine' — November, the ninth month. The same word (from novus) also means new.

vingt.etymology_derivation: Latin vīgintī — English 'vigesimal' (counting by twenties) is the same root; French just kept counting that way: quatre-vingts.

ans.context_translation: I'm thirty years old (I have thirty years).
ans.etymology_derivation: Latin annus — annual, anniversary. Age is something you have in French: j'ai X ans.

lundi.etymology_derivation: Moon-day, exactly like English Monday — both calendars still worship the moon.

mardi.etymology_derivation: Mars' day. English named Tuesday after Tiw, but mardi gras kept the Mars in the calendar.

janvier.etymology_derivation: Janus, the two-faced god of doors and beginnings — in-month uses en, not dans.

aujourdhui.etymology_derivation: 'on the day of today' — hui is Latin hodiē ('on this day') worn down to a suffix. Today's today, recursively.

semaine.etymology_derivation: Latin septimāna, the seven-morning stretch. English had the same coin: sennight, seven nights — now extinct.

mangé.etymology_derivation: manger ← Latin manducāre 'to chew'. English 'mange' is the eating disease — the verb came with the Normans' dogs.

décidé.etymology_derivation: dé·cidé — the é IS the -ed. Decided, désigné, marié: the participle twins are everywhere.

parlé.etymology_derivation: parler ← Late Latin parabolāre 'to tell stories' — parable, parley, parliament (the talking-place).

trouvé.etymology_derivation: trover 'to find' — what you found is a trove.

aimé.etymology_derivation: aimer ← ad + estimare 'to estimate'. English 'aim' drifted from the same estimate — aiming is assessing.

fini.etymology_derivation: Latin fīnis 'end, boundary' — finish, final, fine print.

allé.etymology_derivation: aller's participle; motion verbs form their past with être — and the participle agrees: allée, allés, allées.

arrivé.etymology_derivation: Late Latin ad rīpam 'to the shore' — to arrive was to land on a riverbank.

rester.context_translation: I am going to stay here.
rester.etymology_derivation: Latin restāre (to stand back, remain). Takes être in the past (je suis resté).

resté.etymology_derivation: Latin restāre 'to stand back, remain'. Staying counts as motion's family — être-house logic.

monté.etymology_derivation: Latin montem 'mountain' — to go up is to mountain-ward.

venu.etymology_derivation: Latin venīre — venue (where you come), venture, adventure (what you come to).

né.etymology_derivation: Latin nātus — natal, native, nation (the born-together people).

était.etymology_derivation: être's imparfait — the background tense, the was of a story already in motion.

habiter.context_translation: I've lived here for three years.
habiter.etymology_derivation: habitāre 'to dwell often' — a habitat is where a thing dwells; habits are where you dwell repeatedly. With depuis, it stays present tense.

utiliser.context_translation: I used to ride my bike.

plus.etymology_derivation: borrowed into English whole — plus is plus. The final s falls silent in most positions.

meilleur.etymology_derivation: Latin melior — English 'ameliorate'. bon→meilleur is good→better's twin suppletion: both languages froze an old comparative.

lever.context_phrase: Je me lève à sept heures.
lever.etymology_derivation: Latin levāre 'to lift' — lever, levitate, elevate. se lever: you raise yourself.

appeler.context_translation: My name is Marie (I call myself Marie).
appeler.etymology_derivation: ad + pellere 'to drive toward' — an appeal drives someone toward you. je m'appelle: I call myself.

coucher.english_meaning: to lay down; to put to bed
coucher.etymology_derivation: collocāre 'to place together' → couch — the furniture is the verb, frozen.

table.etymology_derivation: Latin tabula 'board, plank'. English borrowed the French word whole — remember it is feminine: la table.

commerce.etymology_derivation: Latin commercium (com- 'together' + merx 'merchandise'). Everyday French for local shops and trade.

restaurant.etymology_derivation: From restaurer 'to restore' — originally a restoring broth sold in Paris in 1765.

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin pars minuta prima ('first small part' of an hour). Feminine in French.

moment.etymology_derivation: Latin momentum 'movement, weight that tips the scales'. Noun in -ment is masculine.

désirer.etymology_derivation: Reach up the English register ladder from 'want' to 'desire' and French désirer is standing right there.

demander.context_translation: I want to ask for a table.
demander.etymology_derivation: Latin demandāre 'to entrust'. In French it softened into everyday 'to ask', never aggressive 'demand'.

entrer.context_translation: I want to go in here.
entrer.etymology_derivation: English says 'go in' at home and 'enter' on signs; French uses entrer every day.

arriver.context_translation: The train is going to arrive.

continuer.context_translation: We are going to keep going.

nation.etymology_derivation: Latin nātiō 'birth, tribe'. Feminine like every -ion noun.

décision.etymology_derivation: Latin dēcīsiō 'a cutting off' — deciding cuts away the alternatives.

conversation.etymology_derivation: Latin conversātiō 'living together, turning with someone'.

expliquer.etymology_derivation: explication → expliquer (c turns to qu before e to keep the /k/ sound).

finir.context_translation: I want to finish my coffee.
finir.etymology_derivation: French 2nd conjugation (-ir) extended plurals with -iss- (nous finissons), which English borrowed as -ish: finish, punish, abolish.

choisir.context_translation: You are going to choose the cake.
choisir.etymology_derivation: Frankish *kausjan (cousin of English choose) entered French as an -ir verb.

vendre.context_translation: They want to sell the house.
vendre.etymology_derivation: Latin vendere — English kept it in vendor and vending machine.

répondre.etymology_derivation: Latin respondēre 'to pledge back'. Notice the dropped s turns into the acute accent on é.

attendre.context_translation: I am waiting for the train.
attendre.etymology_derivation: Latin attendere 'to stretch toward'. In French it means to wait for — with no preposition 'for' needed!

jamais.etymology_derivation: Latin iam magis 'ever more'. Paired with ne, it means 'never'.

rien.etymology_derivation: Latin rem 'a thing' (root of real, republic). Just like pas ('a step'), a positive noun turned negative by company with ne.

plus_neg.context_phrase: Je ne veux plus de café.
plus_neg.etymology_derivation: When wrapped inside ne...plus, the final s is silent and the meaning flips from 'more' to 'no more / no longer'.

il.etymology_derivation: Latin ille 'that man' — the same word that gave le.

nous.etymology_derivation: Latin nōs — English keeps the root in nostrum.

êtes.etymology_derivation: Old French estes → êtes: the circumflex hat marks the vanished s.

là.etymology_derivation: Grave accent distinguishes là ('there') from la ('the/her').

content.etymology_derivation: Latin contentus. Feminine wakes the silent t: contente /kɔ̃tɑ̃t/.

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

expérience.etymology_derivation: Also means 'scientific experiment' in a lab.

chance.etymology_derivation: Late Latin cadentia 'the falling of dice' (doublet of cadence).

finalement.context_translation: In the end, we stay here.
finalement.etymology_derivation: finale + -ment — the true French word for English 'eventually'.

terrible.etymology_derivation: In spoken French, 'C'est terrible !' can even mean 'terrific!'.

quand.etymology_derivation: Latin quandō. In liaison before a vowel, the d sounds like /t/: quand il arrive /kɑ̃.t‿il/.

combien.etymology_derivation: When followed by a noun, takes bare de: combien de temps ('how much time').

quel.etymology_derivation: Agrees with its noun: quel (m), quelle (f), quels (mpl), quelles (fpl) — all four sound identical (/kɛl/)!

parce_que.etymology_derivation: Pourquoi asks 'for what?'; parce que answers 'by that which'.

professeur.etymology_derivation: Used for any school or university teacher.

erreur.etymology_derivation: Like la couleur, l'erreur kept its Latin feminine gender from abstract qualities.

peur.context_translation: I am afraid (lit. I have fear).
peur.etymology_derivation: Latin pavor → peur. Feminine abstract noun.

fleur.etymology_derivation: Latin flōrem → French fleur → English flower.

heure.etymology_derivation: Latin hōra. Silent H triggers elision: l'heure.

voulez.etymology_derivation: Every French verb (except être, dire, faire) ends in -ez with vous!

français.etymology_derivation: Not capitalized when naming the language in French.

as.etymology_derivation: Pronounced /a/ — the final s stays silent unless followed by a vowel.

a.etymology_derivation: No accent on a ('has') vs grave accent on à ('to/at').

avez.etymology_derivation: In liaison, the s of vous buzzes as /z/: vous‿avez /vu.za.ve/.

hôpital.etymology_derivation: Compare hospital and hôtel — the circumflex on ô marks the vanished s!

hiver.etymology_derivation: Latin tempus hībernum 'wintry season' — English hibernate.

histoire.etymology_derivation: One French word covers both 'history' and 'story'.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.

jardin.etymology_derivation: Frankish *gardo gave English garden/yard and French jardin.

beau.etymology_derivation: BAGS adjective: steps before the noun! Becomes bel before a vowel (un bel hôtel) and belle in the feminine.

nouveau.etymology_derivation: Steps before the noun; nouvel before a vowel, nouvelle in the feminine.

jeune.etymology_derivation: Already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine are identical.

vieux.etymology_derivation: Becomes vieil before a vowel (un vieil ami) and vieille in the feminine.

noir.etymology_derivation: Placed after the noun, like all color adjectives.

allons.etymology_derivation: Regular stem all- returns in nous allons and vous allez.

allez.etymology_derivation: Also shouted at sports matches: 'Allez !' ('Come on!').

demain.context_translation: Tomorrow, I'm going to visit Lyon.

voir.context_translation: I'm going to see my friend.
voir.etymology_derivation: Latin vidēre lost its middle d: vedere → veoir → voir.

faire.context_translation: What are you going to do?
faire.etymology_derivation: One French verb covers both 'do' and 'make' (like Spanish hacer and German machen).

au.etymology_derivation: Never *à le: French fuses them into au (/o/). Plural à + les = aux.

du.etymology_derivation: Does double duty: 'from the' (du train) and the masculine partitive 'some' (du pain, du café).

des.etymology_derivation: Plural of un/une: where English says bare 'books', French says des livres ('some books').

pour.etymology_derivation: Followed by an infinitive, pour means 'in order to': pour comprendre ('in order to understand').

vin.context_translation: I would like some red wine.

fromage.etymology_derivation: Latin caseus formāticus ('cheese made in a form/mold') — French kept the mold word!

soupe.etymology_derivation: Takes feminine partitive de la: de la soupe.

mon.context_phrase: C'est mon père et mon amie.
mon.context_translation: It's my father and my (female) friend.
mon.etymology_derivation: Also steps in before feminine nouns starting with a vowel (mon opinion, mon idée) to avoid a vowel clash!

ma.etymology_derivation: Used before feminine singular nouns starting with a consonant.

mes.etymology_derivation: One plural form for both genders.

son.shift_rule: Agrees with the thing owned, NOT the owner
son.context_translation: Marie is looking for her brother.
son.etymology_derivation: The biggest English-transfer trap: son frère can mean 'his brother' OR 'her brother' because frère is masculine!

sa.shift_rule: Agrees with the thing owned, NOT the owner
sa.etymology_derivation: Paul is male, but maison is feminine, so it MUST be sa maison!

ce.etymology_derivation: Becomes cet before a vowel (cet hôtel) and cette in the feminine (cette table).

moi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions (avec moi, chez moi, pour moi) and in C'est moi.

toi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions: pour toi, chez toi.

six.etymology_derivation: Final x sounds like /s/ alone, is silent before a consonant (six jours /si ʒuʁ/), and buzzes as /z/ before a vowel (six ans /si.z‿ɑ̃/).

quatre_vingts.etymology_derivation: Literally 'four-twenties', just like Abraham Lincoln's 'four score'. And 90 is quatre-vingt-dix ('four-twenty-ten')!

jeudi.etymology_derivation: Jupiter's day — the Roman counterpart to Thor's Thursday.

vendredi.etymology_derivation: Venus's day — counterpart to Freya's Friday.

dimanche.etymology_derivation: Latin dies Dominica 'Day of the Lord'. Placing le before a weekday means 'every [weekday]'.

juillet.etymology_derivation: Months take en ('en juillet'), while specific dates take le ('le quatorze juillet').

compris.etymology_derivation: prendre → pris, comprendre → compris, apprendre → appris.

pris.etymology_derivation: French uses prendre ('to take') for ordering food and drink, just like English 'I'll take a coffee'.

vu.context_translation: I have already seen this film.
vu.etymology_derivation: English already owns this participle inside 'déjà vu'!

déjà.etymology_derivation: You already know it from déjà vu ('already seen').

parti.etymology_derivation: partir takes être in the past: je suis parti(e).

sorti.context_phrase: Elle est sortie avec ses amis.
sorti.context_translation: She went out with her friends.
sorti.etymology_derivation: sortir takes être in the past.

avais.english_meaning: had, used to have (j'avais / tu avais)
avais.context_translation: I used to have a small car.
avais.etymology_derivation: Imparfait paints the ongoing background setting.

habitais.etymology_derivation: Take the nous stem (habit-) and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

voulais.context_translation: I wanted to talk to you.
voulais.etymology_derivation: Used for ongoing past desires or polite softening ('I was wanting to ask...').

depuis.context_translation: I have lived here for three years (lit. I live here since three years).
depuis.etymology_derivation: Because the action is still true right now, French uses the PRESENT tense with depuis!

aussi.context_phrase: Elle est aussi grande que son frère.
aussi.context_translation: She is as tall as her brother.
aussi.etymology_derivation: Inside comparisons, aussi + adjective + que means 'as [adj] as'.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

en_pron.english_meaning: of it, of them, some, any
en_pron.context_phrase: Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux.
en_pron.context_translation: Do you want coffee? — Yes, I want some (of it).
en_pron.etymology_derivation: Whenever a verb or quantity uses de/du/de la/des, en replaces the whole phrase and walks left of the verb!

y.context_phrase: Tu vas à Paris ? — Oui, j'y vais.
y.context_translation: Are you going to Paris? — Yes, I'm going there.
y.etymology_derivation: Replaces any place phrase introduced by à, en, dans, or chez.

me.etymology_derivation: Elides to m' before a vowel: il m'écoute.

te.etymology_derivation: Elides to t' before a vowel: je t'aime.

lui.context_translation: I speak to him / to her.
lui.etymology_derivation: One single pronoun means BOTH 'to him' and 'to her' before a verb!

leur.etymology_derivation: Before a verb, leur means 'to them' and NEVER takes an -s.

laver.english_meaning: to wash (se laver: to wash oneself)
laver.etymology_derivation: Notice French uses the reflexive + definite article for body parts: je me lave les mains.

il_y_a.english_meaning: there is, there are; ago (with time)
il_y_a.context_phrase: Il y a un bon bistro ici.
il_y_a.context_translation: There is a good bistro here.
il_y_a.etymology_derivation: With a spatial noun it means 'there is/are'; with a time span (il y a trois jours) it means 'three days ago'!

voudrais.context_phrase: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
voudrais.context_translation: I would like a croissant, please.
voudrais.etymology_derivation: Future stem voudr- + imparfait ending -ais = the polite conditional!

faut.english_meaning: is necessary (il faut: one must / it is needed)
faut.context_translation: We/you have to leave now (lit. It is necessary to leave).
faut.etymology_derivation: From Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — what is lacking is what is needed! Only ever used with il.

soit.context_phrase: Il faut que ce soit prêt.
soit.etymology_derivation: English borrowed this subjunctive twice: 'soit!' and the motto 'Honi soit qui mal y pense'.

savoir.english_meaning: to know (facts, how to do something)
savoir.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, information, and skills (je sais + infinitive, without 'how').

connaître.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places)
connaître.etymology_derivation: Always takes a noun object (a person, city, book, or restaurant).

qui.context_phrase: L'homme qui parle est mon père.
qui.context_translation: The man who is speaking is my father.
qui.etymology_derivation: Followed directly by the verb. Never drops its i before a vowel!

dont.context_phrase: C'est le film dont je parle.
dont.context_translation: That's the film I'm talking about (lit. of which I speak).
dont.etymology_derivation: Whenever the verb takes de (parler de, avoir besoin de), French uses dont.

venir.etymology_derivation: Prefix it to build a whole family: revenir (come back), devenir (become), prévenir (warn).

revenir.context_translation: I'm going to come back tomorrow.

tenir.etymology_derivation: Conjugates exactly like venir (je tiens, je viens).

maintenir.etymology_derivation: Literally 'to hold in the hand' (main + tenir)!

comprendre.etymology_derivation: To understand is literally 'to grasp together'.

apprendre.etymology_derivation: An apprentice is literally 'one who is learning'.

faim.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have hunger).
faim.etymology_derivation: French possesses physical states with avoir: avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir froid, avoir chaud, avoir raison.

soif.etymology_derivation: Used with avoir without an article: avoir soif.

raison.context_translation: You are right (lit. You have reason).
raison.etymology_derivation: To be right in French is to 'have reason'.

besoin.context_translation: I need help (lit. I have need of help).
besoin.etymology_derivation: Triggers dont in relative clauses because of its built-in de.

droite.context_translation: The station is on the right.

gare.etymology_derivation: Originally a river shelter where boats pulled in.

train.context_phrase: Le train part à huit heures.
train.etymology_derivation: Old French traïn 'a line of things pulled along'.

billet.etymology_derivation: Double ll after i sounds like /j/.

addition.etymology_derivation: The restaurant bill is literally 'the addition' of the prices.

livre.etymology_derivation: Masculine le livre is 'the book'; feminine la livre is 'the pound'!

cinéma.context_phrase: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
cinéma.context_translation: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?
cinéma.etymology_derivation: Invented by the Lumière brothers in Lyon in 1895.

tête.etymology_derivation: Latin testa 'terracotta pot' — Roman slang for the skull! The circumflex marks the vanished s.

manteau.etymology_derivation: Old French mantel → manteau; English kept 'mantle'.

robe.etymology_derivation: In everyday French, une robe is any woman's dress.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.

compounds.lore: gratter 'to scrape' + ciel 'sky' (Latin caelum). English reached for the same image: the thing that scrapes the sky.
tirer 'to pull' + bouchon 'cork' (bouche 'mouth'). The tool named by its two movements.
porter 'to carry' + feuille 'leaf/sheet' — the folder of sheets. English borrowed the same compound as portfolio and promoted it to finance.
ouvrir 'to open' + boîte 'box'. French builds tools as verb-object; English as noun-noun.
laver + vaisselle (from vaissel 'vessels', Latin vascellum). The machine named as a sentence.
parer 'to shield' + brise 'breeze'. English's windshield shields the wind; French's shields the breeze — same thought, opposite word order.
porter + monnaie 'coins' (Latin moneta, the mint goddess Juno Moneta — 'money' is a temple's name).
compounds.example_sentence: Il y a cinq euros dans le porte-monnaie.
compounds.example_translation: There are five euros in the purse.

compounds.lore: casser 'to break' + croûte 'crust'. A snack is a broken crust — the verb inside names the eater.
sécher + cheveux 'hair' (Latin capillus — 'capillary' is the same hair).
porter + parole 'word' (Latin parabola — the story-word of parlé). The one who carries the words.
parer 'to ward off' + pluie 'rain' — built just like parasol ('ward-off-sun') and pare-brise ('ward-off-breeze').
chauve 'bald' + souris 'mouse' — because a bat's wings have no fur.
pomme 'apple/fruit' + de terre 'of earth'. When tubers arrived from the Andes, French named them apples of the soil.
compounds.example_sentence: Une soupe de pommes de terre.

compounds.lore: après 'after' + midi 'mid-day (noon)' — an exact calque of English afternoon.
dé- 'un-' + jeûner 'to fast' = literally 'break-fast'! When midday took over déjeuner, morning became le petit-déjeuner.
compounds.example_sentence: Je prends le petit-déjeuner à huit heures.
compounds.example_translation: I have breakfast at eight o'clock.

compounds.lore: coup 'blow/stroke' + de foudre 'of lightning'. Falling in love at first sight is being struck by lightning.
compounds.example_translation: It was love at first sight.

falseFriends.trap_note: actuellement is time, not truth: 'je travaille actuellement à Paris' = 'I'm currently working in Paris'. The actually you want is en fait (in fact).
assister à un concert means you watched it, not helped it. Assisting is aider.
j'attends le train = I'm waiting for the train. Attending a class is suivre (to follow) un cours.
blesser hurts: il s'est blessé = he got injured. Blessing is bénir.
demander is the everyday 'to ask' — no aggression inside. Demanding is exiger.
falseFriends.example_translation: I'm going to ask for directions.

falseFriends.trap_note: the librairie sells books. The lending library is la bibliothèque.
falseFriends.example_sentence: J'achète des livres à la librairie.
falseFriends.example_translation: I buy books at the bookshop.

falseFriends.trap_note: monnaie is the change in your pocket. Money as a concept is l'argent.
la notice is the leaflet of instructions. A posted notice is un avis.
sensible means feeling things deeply. The sensible one is raisonnable.
éventuellement opens a possibility. Eventually is finalement — at the end of time, not in the realm of maybe.
une bonne éducation is good manners, not good grades. Schooling is l'instruction or les études.
un coin is a corner — the metal coins are pièces. 'Mon coin' is my neck of the woods.
falseFriends.example_sentence: Le chat dort dans son coin.
falseFriends.example_translation: The cat sleeps in its corner.

falseFriends.trap_note: le raisin is a fresh grape on the vine (and produces le vin). A dried raisin is un raisin sec ('a dry grape').
Bonne journée ! means 'Have a good day!', not 'Have a good trip!'. A travel journey is un voyage.
une voiture de location is a rental car. A geographic location or spot is un lieu or un endroit.
In modern French, C'est formidable ! is high praise ('That's wonderful!'), with zero fear attached.
